articles.title: Oil catch-up: Iran says tanker hit mine in Hormuz; Centcom says drone struck it instead
articles.description: The dispute adds fresh uncertainty to an already fragile Strait of Hormuz transit corridor, a chokepoint for a large share of global seaborne oil. Whether the vessel was disabled by a mine or by direct missile and drone strikes matters for risk pricing: a live minefield implies a broader navigational hazard for all shipping, while a targeted strike suggests continued deliberate Iranian action against specific vessels. Either reading keeps war-risk premiums and freight costs elevated, with the tanker-hire market already under pressure from the wider conflict. Oil markets are likely to treat the incident as another reminder that safe-passage assurances through Hormuz remain unreliable, regardless of which account proves accurate. Iran and the US are offering flatly contradictory accounts of what disabled a burning tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran blaming a mine and Washington blaming its own forces' missile and drone strikes. Summary: Iran's IRGC Navy, cited by IRNA, says a tanker exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine while attempting to transit a restricted route south of the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC says the fire could not be contained and the vessel is now fully engulfed in flames; it says prior warnings had been issued about the route. US Central Command disputes the mine claim, identifying the vessel as the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia. Centcom says El Gaia was struck by an Iranian missile last month, which disabled it, and was hit again by an Iranian drone this past weekend while sitting in waters off the coast of Oman. Reports indicate the tanker's crew, understood to be Indian nationals, were evacuated, with one crew member unaccounted for. The incident adds to a run of tanker attacks and disputed claims around the Strait of Hormuz amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy says a tanker has exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine while attempting to transit a restricted southern route through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a statement carried by state news agency IRNA. The IRGC said efforts to bring the blaze under control had failed and that the vessel was now completely engulfed in flames, adding that it had previously warned ships against using what it called an illegal passage. US Central Command has rejected that account. In a statement, Centcom identified the vessel as the Panama-flagged oil tanker El Gaia and said it was not struck by a mine at all. Instead, the command said the tanker was disabled by an Iranian missile strike last month, then hit a second time by an Iranian drone this past weekend while sitting in waters off the coast of Oman. The competing versions leave the actual cause of the tanker's condition unresolved, with Tehran and Washington offering accounts that cannot both be accurate. The El Gaia's crew, reported to be Indian nationals, were evacuated during the more recent incident, with one crew member said to be unaccounted for as of the latest reports. Neither side's account has been independently verified by maritime monitoring organisations at the time of writing. The episode is the latest in a string of disputed tanker incidents in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Iran's conflict escalated earlier this year. Iran has repeatedly claimed mine strikes on vessels transiting the waterway, while US forces have said on multiple occasions that mines cleared from internationally recognised shipping lanes make such claims implausible, characterising them instead as disinformation intended to intimidate commercial shipping. Whether the cause proves to be a mine or a direct strike, the incident underscores that the Strait of Hormuz, a corridor carrying a significant share of the world's seaborne oil, remains a live risk zone for shipping. With war-risk premiums already elevated and tanker hire rates under pressure, further disputed incidents of this kind are likely to keep freight costs high and reinforce caution among operators considering transit through the strait. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
